title: Adverb Placement: Front and Mid Position
summary: Choose front or mid position for connecting, time, place, comment, degree, sequence and frequency adverbs; recognise the contrast between a speaker’s comment and the manner of an action, and avoid inserting long adverbials unnaturally inside verb phrases.
learningObjectives: Place connecting, time-setting and comment adverbs at the front when they relate the whole clause to what precedes it.
Distinguish a front-position sentence comment from an end-position manner description using the same adverb.
Position typical degree, sequencing and indefinite-frequency adverbs in the middle of a clause, including with auxiliaries and forms of be.
Recognise placement restrictions on certain degree adverbs and long adverbials, and move items to the front for emphasis without distorting their meaning.

explanation.heading: Connecting ideas and establishing a scene at the front
explanation.body: Front-position adverbs and adverbials can link a new sentence to an earlier claim, locate a later event in time or space, or frame the writer’s next point. Consequently and nevertheless often signal a logical relation; later that evening or at the entrance creates a setting. The comma in writing helps mark the frame. Front placement is common rather than compulsory: the discourse purpose decides whether the opening deserves emphasis.
explanation.example: The data were incomplete. Consequently, the committee delayed its recommendation.

explanation.heading: Comment on the whole clause versus manner of one action
explanation.body: Clearly, naturally, seriously, frankly and similar words can function as comment adverbs at the front, conveying a judgment about the entire statement. At the end, a manner use describes how the event happened. Changing position can alter what the speaker communicates: Frankly, she answered the question evaluates the act of speaking from the speaker’s perspective; She answered the question frankly describes her candid manner. Some sentences allow more than one interpretation, so supply enough context.
explanation.example: Naturally, the new arrivals needed directions; the instructor then explained the route naturally, without reading a script.

explanation.heading: Mid-position degree adverbs and verb compatibility
explanation.body: Almost, hardly, nearly, quite, rather and scarcely commonly appear in mid position, typically before the main lexical verb, after the first auxiliary or after be. Several other degree adverbs, including completely, enormously and greatly, also occur at the end, depending on the verb. Verb combinations impose real restrictions: enormously is natural after grow or differ, whereas enormously differ in mid position is generally not; greatly admired is fine, while greatly care is not a neutral pairing. Placement should be learned together with meaning and collocation.
explanation.example: We almost abandoned the project, but the new funding greatly improved our options.

explanation.heading: Order adverbs and indefinite frequency
explanation.body: First, next and last can mark event order in mid or end position; when an explicit time phrase occurs, the order adverb generally precedes it. At the front, first and next can introduce steps in a list instead. Always, never, often, rarely, seldom and hardly ever generally occur in mid position, although certain frequency adverbs can be fronted for emphasis. Long phrases such as from time to time and on many occasions usually belong at the front or end rather than between auxiliary and main verb.
explanation.example: We first discussed the proposal in April, and we have rarely revisited it since.

explanation.heading: Length, emphasis and natural clause rhythm
explanation.body: Long prepositional phrases, subordinate clauses and extended descriptive adverbials normally sit at the end or are moved to the front when emphasis or connection requires it. They rarely interrupt a verb phrase in mid position. A fronted frequency or degree expression may highlight the whole statement, but its grammatical pattern still matters. Do not assume that every short adverb must be moved to the middle or that every long adverbial can interrupt an auxiliary and a main verb.
explanation.example: With considerable patience, the mediator explained the decision to both groups.

comparisons.title: Comment on a statement versus manner of an action

left.label: Whole-clause comment, often in front
left.example: Honestly, the editor rejected the draft.
left.note: Honestly presents the speaker’s frank assessment of the statement.

right.label: Manner, often at the end
right.example: The editor rejected the draft honestly.
right.note: Honestly describes how the editor carried out the rejection.

comparisons.title: Short frequency adverb versus long frequency phrase

left.label: Indefinite frequency in mid position
left.note: Seldom is a short indefinite-frequency adverb normally placed after the auxiliary.

right.label: Long frequency phrase at the front or end
right.example: From time to time, we receive complaints.
right.note: The multiword adverbial frames the clause instead of interrupting the verb phrase.

examples.sentence: The bridge was closed. Nevertheless, the rescue teams reached the island.
examples.note: Nevertheless connects contrasting statements at the start of the second sentence.

examples.sentence: Strangely, the audience remained completely silent.
examples.note: Strangely comments on the entire situation; completely intensifies silent.

examples.sentence: The researcher first met her supervisor in 2019.
examples.note: First occupies mid position before the lexical verb and precedes the definite time phrase.

examples.sentence: The number of visitors has nearly doubled.
examples.note: Nearly appears after the first auxiliary and before the main participle.

examples.sentence: We analysed the samples with exceptional care.
examples.note: The long manner phrase is natural at the end, not between analysed and the samples.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The survey rarely has revealed such a difference.
commonMistakes.correct: The survey has rarely revealed such a difference.
commonMistakes.why: Place the frequency adverb after the auxiliary has and before the past participle.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The two samples enormously differ in quality.
commonMistakes.correct: The two samples differ enormously in quality.
commonMistakes.why: Enormously is more natural after differ in this construction.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I from time to time have visited the archive.
commonMistakes.correct: From time to time, I have visited the archive.
commonMistakes.why: A long frequency phrase normally goes at the front or end rather than in the middle of the verb group.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The analyst nearly had finished the report.
commonMistakes.correct: The analyst had nearly finished the report.
commonMistakes.why: With this intended meaning of almost completing, nearly is placed after the auxiliary had.

studyTips: For each of clearly, honestly and naturally, write one sentence where the adverb comments on the whole situation and another where it describes manner; explain the difference.
Underline auxiliaries in sentences with frequency and degree adverbs, then practise putting a short adverb between the auxiliary and main verb.
Move long phrases such as on several occasions and with extreme caution to the beginning and end of a sentence; compare which version gives the best emphasis.

exercises.prompt: The original application lacked evidence. Choose the sentence that correctly starts the consequence with a connecting adverb.
choices: Consequently, the panel requested more documents.
The panel consequently requested more documents therefore.
Consequently the panel, requested more documents.
exercises.feedback: Consequently correctly marks the logical result in front position; the other versions misuse punctuation or duplicate the connector.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence where "honestly" clearly comments on the speaker’s assessment of the whole clause, rather than how an action was performed.
choices: The witness answered the question honestly.
The manager described the error honestly.
exercises.feedback: Front-position Honestly, introduces the speaker’s candid judgement of the proposition.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "The audience ___ noticed the quiet change in tone." The change was almost unnoticed.
exercises.feedback: Hardly appears before the main lexical verb noticed in this simple past clause.

exercises.prompt: Which placement is most natural when the intention is to describe a large difference between two estimates?
exercises.feedback: Enormously typically follows differ rather than occurring before it.

exercises.prompt: "We have ___ had to cancel an exhibition." Supply the single indefinite-frequency adverb meaning very infrequently: seldom.
exercises.feedback: A short indefinite-frequency adverb follows have and precedes had.

exercises.prompt: "The route has ___ changed since the inspection." Supply the adverb meaning almost, using the cue "nearly".
exercises.feedback: Nearly is a mid-position degree adverb, after has and before changed.

exercises.prompt: "The curator ___ examined the letters in 2020." Supply the ordering adverb meaning before doing anything else: first.
exercises.feedback: First can come before the lexical verb examined and before the time phrase.

exercises.prompt: "___, the revised map was easier to read." Supply the front-position connector that introduces a contrasting point: Nevertheless.
exercises.feedback: Nevertheless is a front-position connecting adverb contrasting with a previous claim.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the adverb placement: "The team always has used paper forms."
acceptedAnswers: The team has always used paper forms.
exercises.feedback: Always normally follows the first auxiliary and precedes the main participle.

exercises.prompt: Correct the unnatural mid-position degree adverb: "These paintings enormously vary in size."
acceptedAnswers: These paintings vary enormously in size.

exercises.prompt: Move the long frequency adverbial to a natural front position: "She from time to time attends the evening talks."
acceptedAnswers: From time to time, she attends the evening talks.
exercises.feedback: Long frequency phrases normally frame the clause or follow it instead of interrupting it.

exercises.prompt: Correct the degree adverb position while keeping the intended meaning: "We completely have revised the timetable."
acceptedAnswers: We have completely revised the timetable.
exercises.feedback: With present perfect have, the adverb usually comes before the lexical participle.

speakingExercises.prompt: Connect two ideas. Say the full second sentence beginning with "Consequently". Facts: The venue lost power / the ceremony was postponed. Give only the consequence sentence.
speakingExercises.feedback: The connector occupies front position and relates the postponement to the earlier cause.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a frank comment on the whole statement. Facts: the explanation / be / incomplete. Start with "Honestly".
speakingExercises.feedback: Front-position Honestly indicates the speaker’s candid assessment.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a near event with mid-position degree. Facts: We / almost / miss / the train. Use the past simple.
speakingExercises.feedback: Almost comes before the lexical verb missed.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a rare activity. Facts: I / hardly ever / eat / at that restaurant. Use the present simple.
acceptedAnswers: I hardly ever eat at that restaurant.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hardly ever is a mid-position indefinite-frequency expression.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe the degree of difference. Facts: Their results / differ / enormously. Use the present simple.
speakingExercises.feedback: With differ, enormously naturally occupies end position.

speakingExercises.prompt: Put the long phrase first and give a complete sentence. Facts: On several occasions / we / have / raised / this concern. Use the present perfect.
acceptedAnswers: On several occasions, we have raised this concern.
speakingExercises.feedback: The long frequency phrase goes at the beginning instead of between have and raised.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the adverb position aloud: "The panel rarely has considered alternatives."
acceptedAnswers: The panel has rarely considered alternatives.
speakingExercises.feedback: Rarely belongs after the auxiliary has in this sentence.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two sentences in the given order with full verb forms. Sentence one: I / first / visited / the gallery / in June. Sentence two: I / have / seldom / returned / since.
acceptedAnswers: I first visited the gallery in June. I have seldom returned since.
speakingExercises.feedback: First precedes the lexical verb in the past clause, and seldom follows the auxiliary in the present perfect.

listeningExercises.audioText: The inspection failed. Consequently, the organisers closed the hall until the repairs were complete.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the organisers close the hall?
choices: An inspection failure led to the closure.
The repairs were complete before the inspection.
The organisers opened the hall for a celebration.
listeningExercises.feedback: Consequently links the closure to the unsuccessful inspection.

listeningExercises.audioText: Frankly, I do not believe this timetable is practical, although the team submitted it confidently.
choices: Show how quickly the team worked.
listeningExercises.feedback: Frankly comments on the entire claim that the timetable is impractical.

listeningExercises.audioText: The committee has rarely changed its membership during the past decade.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two-word frequency-and-verb phrase heard directly after "has".
listeningExercises.feedback: Rarely comes before the lexical participle changed.

listeningExercises.audioText: We first reviewed the drawings in February, and only later examined the final prototype.
listeningExercises.feedback: First marks the earlier event; only later introduces the subsequent one.

listeningExercises.audioText: The designs differ enormously in cost, but their dimensions are nearly identical.
choices: There is a major cost difference but almost no difference in size.
The designs cost the same and vary a lot in size.
The dimensions and costs are both identical.
listeningExercises.feedback: Enormously strengthens differ; nearly identical describes very similar dimensions.

listeningExercises.audioText: From time to time, the curator invites local artists to discuss their work.
listeningExercises.prompt: How frequently do the invitations occur?
listeningExercises.feedback: From time to time is a multiword adverbial meaning occasionally.

listeningExercises.audioText: The team has almost completed the restoration.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two-word degree-and-verb phrase heard after "has".
listeningExercises.feedback: Almost normally comes between has and the main participle completed.

listeningExercises.audioText: In contrast, the museum accepted the revised terms.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the two-word connecting phrase heard before "the museum".
listeningExercises.feedback: In contrast is a front-position linking expression that connects an opposing idea to earlier context.
